entries.test: The public recording or transcript of Amodei's statement would show whether he supplied evidence supporting the prediction.
entries.note: The claim being assessed is Marcus's assertion that evidence was absent, not Amodei's prediction.
The normalization drops 'I think most or all.' The unspecified points and 'stand the test of time' supply no shared test.

entries.test: The Guardian's account and the seven participants' resulting games would show whether their attempts produced functioning Pac-Man clones.
entries.note: The surrounding paragraphs give 'things didn’t go well' a concrete referent.

entries.test: Representative surveys of trained programmers would show whether a majority adopted AI in their workflows after publication.
entries.note: 'Soon' supplies no explicit deadline; majority adoption is an observable outcome.

entries.test: Controlled studies comparing programmer productivity with and without contemporary AI coding tools would show whether those tools produce a modest improvement.
entries.note: 'Increase productivity' attributes an effect to the tools.
Helping with APIs is a capability claim, but the bundled programming-language claim is explicitly hedged with 'maybe.'

entries.test: Public evaluations of tools available in March 2025 would show whether they could reliably handle debugging, architecture, and client requirements without human understanding of those tasks.
entries.note: 'Current' refers to tools available when the post was published.

entries.test: Public longitudinal evaluations of March 2025 AI coding tools on complex repositories would show whether substantial maintenance challenges remained.
entries.note: 'Magically' adds emphasis; the factual commitment is that maintenance challenges remain.

entries.test: Public studies or documented cases with code audits would show whether beginners' excessive reliance on AI tools caused hard-to-maintain code and security problems.
entries.note: This predicts a causal outcome in some cases without setting a deadline.

entries.test: Public employment and software-production evidence would show whether AI eliminated the continuing need for coders and software architects.
entries.note: Calling the idea 'absurd' expresses a substantive rejection of occupational replacement.

entries.test: Public evidence of software-production practices and autonomous coding capabilities would show whether AI remained an aid or replaced people responsible for conceiving, writing, and debugging software.

entries.note: This is a rhetorical challenge, not an asserted probability forecast. The normalization also turns an 'if' premise into an established general inability.
'My guess' explicitly hedges the claim, which includes causal explanations. 'Scarce training examples' broadens the specific reference to fewer Stack Overflow queries.
